tier_reason: Peer-reviewed (ACM TALG 2022, ALENEX 2021); the TALG abstract quoted in the artifact repo README states the la_vector select is the fastest and its rank is on the space-time Pareto frontier against many established compressed rank/select dictionaries (SDSL structures incl. s18_vector, rle_vector). The artifact repo (my_benchmark.cpp, run_all.sh) states gcc 9.2.1, Release plus -march=native and the Xeon E5-2407 v2, which would meet A, but no result numbers are in the repo and the paper PDFs (ACM, boffa.top) are blocked here, so the numbers stay unseen.

corrections.claimed_speedup: TALG 2022 abstract (quoted in the artifact repo README): 'our select is the fastest, and our rank is on the space-time Pareto frontier' versus many well-established compressed rank/select dictionary implementations. No numbers seen here; a search snippet of the paper says LA-vector select is roughly 50 ns slower than sdsl::sd_vector in some configuration, so the win is dataset-dependent (snippet only).
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (ALENEX 2021, ACM TALG 2022), but neither paper could be opened here (ACM and boffa.top blocked), and the artifact repo commits no result CSVs, so the claimed advantage over SDSL is qualitative (abstract) only. A search snippet indicates select can be ~50 ns slower than sdsl::sd_vector on some data, so the advantage is a space-time trade-off, not a uniform speedup. Artifact repo is GPL-3.0 while the library itself is Apache-2.0. Depends on sdsl-lite.

notes: Library and benchmark repos exist and match the record (Apache-2.0, 47 stars, last commit 2024-09-04, stale). An environment that reaches dl.acm.org or boffa.top/files/ALENEX.pdf could check the numbers and possibly raise it to A, since the artifact repo states code, compiler, flags and CPU.

tier_reason: The repo's benchmarking/comparison.cc times orzo against pasta-flat and cs-poppy (pasta-toolbox) rank/select with clang++-17 -O3 -flto -mavx2 (Makefile), but no results or CPU model are published in the repo; the only number (26.49% space saving) comes from search snippets of the SEA 2025 paper, which is blocked here. Without seeing the paper's figures the peer-reviewed B cannot be confirmed, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++-17 -std=c++23 -O3 -flto -mbmi -mbmi2 -mavx2 -static (Makefile; an AVX-512 variant is commented out for the Zaratan cluster)
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (SEA 2025, LIPIcs vol. 338 paper 23, 'Elias-Fano Compression for Space-Efficient Rank and Select Structures'), but the Dagstuhl PDF is blocked here; the 26.49% space saving is from search snippets only. The win is space, not speed: rank must decode Elias-Fano encoded L2 indices, and no speed claim over pasta-flat or cs-poppy was seen. Baselines are pasta-toolbox structures, not SDSL or sux. No LICENSE file (raw 404, none shown on the repo page), so reference only. Single commit (2025-05-12), 2 stars.

notes: Real peer-reviewed research code, but it is a space-saving structure with no speed claim; consider keeping it as a documented memory-metric item rather than a faster-than entry. A session that reaches drops.dagstuhl.de could restore B (paper at drops.dagstuhl.de/storage/00lipics/lipics-vol338-sea2025/LIPIcs.SEA.2025.23/LIPIcs.SEA.2025.23.pdf, not opened).

tier_reason: Upgraded: the repo carries the benchmark code (examples/bench.rs, which runs sux-rs Rank9/RankSmall, qwt, bitm and genedex structures), raw result CSVs (evals/rank-laptop.csv, evals/fm.csv), release build with -C target-cpu=native (.cargo/config.toml), rustc via cargo (rust-version 1.93), and the CPU (Intel Core i7-10750H, README and SEA 2026 paper snippet). Exact rustc version is only lower-bounded by rust-version; the paper itself is peer-reviewed at SEA 2026 (LIPIcs).

corrections.baseline: sux-rs Rank9 and RankSmall (Rust implementation of sux), qwt RSNarrow/RSWide/RSQVector, bitm RankSelect101111 and genedex rank structures; for the FM-index: genedex and AWRY
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc (rust-version 1.93, edition 2024) via cargo run -r; -C target-cpu=native from .cargo/config.toml; AVX2 only
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H (6 cores, hyper-threading), fixed at 3.0 GHz; 1, 6 and 12 threads (README; paper snippet says all experiments ran on this CPU). evals/rank-server.csv is from an unnamed 48/96-thread server.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: BiRank and QuadRank 'up to 2x faster than other methods in high-throughput settings'; QuadFm 'up to 4x faster than genedex'. From evals/rank-laptop.csv at n=2^35 bits, 12 threads, prefetched stream mode: BiRank (BinaryBlock16, 3.3% overhead) 2.63 ns/query vs sux Rank9 4.92 ns and RankSmall<1,11> 5.71 ns, i.e. 1.9x and 2.2x (derived from page data); single-thread latency is not better (94.66 vs 89.42 ns for Rank9). QuadRank 2.6-2.7 ns vs qwt RSQVector256 5.68-6.79 ns in the same mode (derived from page data). evals/fm.csv: best QuadFm 0.156 s vs best genedex 0.312 s at 12 threads (2.0x) and 0.988 vs 2.463 s at 1 thread (2.5x); up to 5.3x vs the slowest genedex configuration (derived from page data). Paper snippet: about 1.5x and 2x faster than similar-overhead methods without interleaving, plus about 2x more from prefetching.
corrections.caveats: Rust crate (callable from C++ only via FFI). Peer-reviewed at SEA 2026 (LIPIcs), but the paper, blog and Dagstuhl pages are blocked here; claims checked against the repo's committed CSVs. The speedup is for batched/prefetched high-throughput queries; single-query latency is on par with or slightly worse than sux Rank9. The sux baseline is sux-rs (Rust), not the C++ sux, and SDSL is not compared. The paper says SPIDER is about as fast; the repo includes its own BinaryBlock16Spider variant. No LICENSE file; MIT comes from Cargo.toml. AVX2 only. Exact rustc version not stated (rust-version 1.93 is the minimum).

notes: Strong evidence: raw CSVs plus bench code against sux-rs Rank9/RankSmall, qwt and genedex. Upgraded B to A; if the orchestrator requires an exact compiler version for A, B (SEA 2026 peer review) is the fallback.
